questions.q: With the page's default settings — prevalence 2%, sensitivity 90%, false positive rate 9% — what is $P(\text{Sick} \mid \text{Positive})$?
questions.explain: $\frac{0.9 \cdot 0.02}{0.9 \cdot 0.02 + 0.09 \cdot 0.98} = \frac{0.018}{0.1062} \approx 0.169$. 90% confuses $P(\text{Positive} \mid \text{Sick})$ with $P(\text{Sick} \mid \text{Positive})$; 2% is the prior before seeing the test.

questions.q: In natural frequencies, out of 10,000 people (2% sick, 90% sensitivity, 9% false positive rate), how many true and false positives are there?
questions.explain: Sick: $10{,}000 \times 0.02 = 200$, of whom $90\%$ test positive $= 180$. Healthy: $9{,}800 \times 0.09 = 882$ false alarms. False positives outnumber true positives roughly 5 to 1.

questions.q: In Bayes' theorem $P(\text{Sick} \mid \text{Positive}) = \frac{P(\text{Positive} \mid \text{Sick})\,P(\text{Sick})}{P(\text{Positive})}$, how is the denominator $P(\text{Positive})$ computed?
questions.explain: By the law of total probability, positives come from two groups: sick people who are detected and healthy people who are falsely flagged. Each conditional rate must be weighted by the group's size.

questions.q: Why does a positive result on a 90%-sensitive test still leave a low chance of being sick when the disease is rare?
options: Because sensitivity and specificity always add up to 100%
Because the healthy group is so large that even a small false positive rate produces more false alarms than true positives (ignoring this is the Base Rate Fallacy)
Because Bayes' theorem only applies to common diseases
questions.explain: The posterior depends on the balance of prevalence and false positive rate. When sick people are rare, the false positives from the huge healthy majority swamp the true positives.
